title: The Old Logic Behind China’s New Economic Weapons: complete reading and selected citation audit
status: Developmental research for parent review; not final chapter approval.
counting_rule: One new complete scholarly journal reading, plus four original documents used for selected reference checks. Related June policy brief and overlapping official/Reuters sources remain dependent evidence. A complete article reading does not mean its cited works were read.
source_format_rule: The published PDF and original HTML bytes are preserved separately from derived text and rendered page images. Hashes refer to exact local bytes.
unperformed_work: No row-level replication of China Sanctions Monitor.
No complete audit of all 48 references.
No new interviews, outreach or internal records.
ANU thesis fallback and Lim–Ferguson 2022 article were not acquired or read because the requested published article was recovered.

sources.title: The Old Logic Behind China’s New Economic Weapons
sources.source_type: Published scholarly journal article; publisher section identified as Provocations. No separate verification of the article’s peer-review process.
sources.access_status: Complete published PDF acquired from a George Washington University journal host; PDF explicitly licenses the article under CC BY 4.0.
sources.reading_scope: All printed pages 25–45, including all substantive prose, Figures 1–3, Table 1, and notes 1–48. Cover metadata also read. Visual checks: physical pages 2, 6, 7, 8, 12 and 21 (printed pages 25, 29–31, 35 and 44).
sources.pagination: 22 physical pages: publisher cover is physical page 1; printed pages 25–45 are physical pages 2–22.
sources.empirical_cutoff: Dataset: 2010 through 2025-08-10; later publication date does not extend the data window.
sources.method: Descriptive dataset of 233 individual economic restrictions. Formal measures identified from official Chinese websites; informal measures inferred from credible reporting, timing and interpretation of likely political or security motivation. Chinese-language legal scholarship and selected episodes develop mechanism hypotheses.

reported_results.status: Authors’ reported counts, printed pp. 28–30; underlying row-level dataset not downloaded or independently recoded.

decisive_locators.content: Hybrid formal/informal framing; definition and ascertainment of measures; dataset cutoff and non-exhaustiveness.
Formalization, countersanction classification, reported counts, Taiwan concentration and alternative explanations.
Domestic principal–agent coordination and foreign threat legibility hypotheses.
2018/2025 comparison; formal and informal restrictions; April 4 dating; Geneva statement interpretation.
Discretion over enforcement; licensing rather than total prohibition; ambiguous relief conditions; compellence/deterrence alternatives.
Conditional future evolution and continuing hybrid model.
Complete citation apparatus, source dependencies and selected reference errors.

sources.supports: Formalization can coexist with enforcement discretion and ambiguity about conditions for relief. Offers a descriptive challenge to treating all growth in formal restrictions as increasing proactive initiation. Supplies coordination, credibility and flexibility mechanisms for testing.
limits: Individual restrictions are not independent negotiations, economic cost estimates or observations of bargaining success.
Official and inferred measures differ in observability; authors acknowledge incomplete earlier coverage; 2025 is a partial year.
No independent dataset replication undertaken here.
Mechanisms are argued with illustrative material; no private instructions establish why a particular licensing application was delayed or approved.
Comparison with Western or democratic sanctions systems is not a matched cross-country test of enforcement or legal predictability.
The 2010 starting date cannot establish a transition from Solomon’s 1967–1984 baseline.
Complete reading of this article is not complete reading of the literature cited in its notes.
independence_and_source_chain: Related to the same authors’ June 18, 2025 policy brief (EC25-12), explicitly cited in note 30; not independent confirmation of overlapping events.
Note 32 cites the Geneva joint statement already acquired as EC25-02.
Note 35 cites the April 4 export-control instrument already acquired as EC25-01.
Note 42 cites the Reuters licensing-process report already acquired as EC25-25.
Chinese legal articles in notes 18–24 are evidence of published scholarly framing, not released negotiating mandates, and were not independently read in this task.
THAAD principal–agent illustration relies on Miura (note 26); Lim and Ferguson 2022 is cited in note 10. Neither work was newly acquired or read here.
critical_reference_checks: Note 43 prints December 5, 2025 for the MFA decision whose original operative date is December 5, 2024: OL25-02.
Note 43 prints April 7, 2025 for the Hudson/Reagan decision whose original operative date is April 7, 2023: OL25-03.
Note 43 prints July 31, 2025 for the McGovern decision whose original operative date is July 31, 2024: OL25-04.
The prose on p. 38 discusses Michael McCaul, but note 43’s congressional citation is about Jim McGovern; it is not a direct source for the prose example.
Note 47 prints January 5, 2025 for the linked BNS/LRT report, dated January 5, 2022 in the original: OL25-05.
These are selected citation checks, not evidence that the dataset uses those erroneous years and not an audit of all references.
Table 1 correctly dates the rare-earth restrictions to April 4; the June policy brief’s erroneous March 14 label is not reproduced in this table.
